notes.meaning: Isaac asked once more whether Jacob was truly Esau, and Jacob answered firmly that he was. Jacob chose to repeat his lie rather than tell the truth to his father. He took advantage of his elderly father's failing senses to secure what had been promised to him.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Some Catholic commentators view Jacob's answer as a sacred mystery rather than an ordinary lie, noting that Jacob was claiming the birthright that legally belonged to him.

notes.meaning: Isaac asked for the wild game to be brought to him so he could eat and then give his blessing. Jacob served the meal and gave him wine to drink. Sharing this formal meal was the traditional setting for officially passing on family leadership to a son.

After finishing the meal, Isaac asked his son to come close and give him a kiss. This kiss was a sign of deep fatherly love and honor. It also gave Isaac one last chance to check his son's identity by touch and smell.

Jacob came close and kissed his father, and Isaac caught the fresh scent of Esau's clothing. Isaac declared that his son smelled like a fruitful field that the Lord had blessed. Convinced by the outdoorsy smell, the aging father was ready to speak the prophetic blessing.

Isaac asked God to give his son plenty of dew from heaven and fertile soil to grow grain and grapes for new wine. In the dry climate of the promised land, heavy morning dew was essential for crops to survive and flourish. This part of the blessing promised rich physical prosperity for the family's future.

Isaac pronounced that entire nations would serve his son, and that he would rule over his brothers. He also repeated God's covenant promise that anyone who cursed him would be cursed, and anyone who blessed him would be blessed. This blessing pointed beyond Jacob's own life to Israel's future kings and ultimately to the Messiah.

Jacob had barely stepped out of his father's presence when Esau returned from his hunt. The timing was remarkably close, showing how narrowly Jacob avoided being caught in the act. Even though human trickery was involved, God ensured the covenant blessing was firmly delivered.

Esau cooked the game he had hunted and brought the dish into his father's tent. He respectfully invited Isaac to sit up and eat so he could receive the promised blessing. Esau was cheerful and confident, fully expecting to receive his father's main inheritance.

Surprised by hearing another person come in, Isaac asked who was speaking. Esau answered directly that he was his firstborn son. This sudden answer made Isaac realize that something was terribly wrong with the blessing he had just finished giving.

Isaac began shaking with uncontrollable trembling as he realized he had blessed Jacob instead of Esau. Yet despite his shock, Isaac declared that the blessing would stand. He realized that God had overruled his personal plans to fulfill the divine purpose, so the spoken word could not be taken back.

When Esau heard his father's words, he cried out with a loud and bitter cry and begged for a blessing of his own. He was devastated to learn that the highest honor had been given to his brother. His tears came from the pain of a lost privilege rather than a heart turning away from sin.

differ.view: Many Methodists teach that Isaac could not change his mind because the blessing was already settled, so Esau was rejected from the covenant blessing rather than from eternal salvation.

notes.meaning: Isaac explained that Jacob had arrived first with deceit and had taken the blessing away. Isaac did not try to hide the craftiness of the scheme, but he acknowledged that the blessing was truly gone. He made it clear to Esau that the transfer was real and could not simply be cancelled.

Esau complained that Jacob lived up to his name, which means one who trips someone up from behind or cheats. He argued that Jacob had now wronged him twice, first taking his birthright and now taking his blessing. In his anger, Esau blamed Jacob completely and refused to admit his own fault in treating the birthright so lightly earlier.

Isaac told Esau that he had already made Jacob master over his relatives and supplied him with grain and wine. The highest authority and provision had been given away under God's inspiration. As a servant of God, Isaac could not invent a second chief blessing or reverse what the Lord had directed.

Esau pleaded with his father, asking if there was really only one blessing available, and he wept loudly. He desperately wanted some kind of fatherly gift or favor. He longed for the physical advantages of the blessing, even though he had never truly valued the spiritual covenant.

Isaac answered with a prophecy about the home where Esau's family would live. While Jacob received the fruitful land of promise, Esau's future in the rugged region of Edom would be far more difficult. His descendants would dwell in a harsh territory that lacked the rich blessings of Canaan.

differ.view: Some evangelicals understand Isaac to be promising Esau fertile soil and dew as a lesser material blessing, while others read the Hebrew as meaning away from rich soil and heavenly dew.

notes.meaning: Isaac told Esau that he would live by the sword and serve his brother, but would eventually break that yoke off his neck. This was fulfilled when the Edomites led a warlike life and became subject to Israel during the reign of King David. Centuries later, Edom revolted against Judah and broke free from their rule.

Esau held a deep hatred against Jacob because of the lost blessing and decided to murder him once their father died. He waited only to spare Isaac the pain of losing a son while alive. Instead of accepting God's will, Esau nursed murderous revenge in the same way Cain had done.

Word of Esau's threats reached Rebekah, and she immediately called Jacob to warn him. She told him that his brother was comforting himself with plans to murder him. Rebekah recognized that Esau's wounded pride had turned into dangerous, deadly rage.

Rebekah told Jacob to listen to her guidance and run away to her brother Laban in Haran. Haran was the ancestral home in northern Mesopotamia where her relatives lived. She urged Jacob to leave quickly before Esau could carry out his violent plan.

She advised Jacob to stay with Laban for a little while until Esau's fierce anger cooled down. Rebekah expected the separation to be short, but it ended up lasting around twenty years. In the end, Rebekah likely never saw her beloved younger son again.

Rebekah hoped to call Jacob back once Esau forgot what had happened, asking why she should lose both sons in a single day. If Esau murdered Jacob, the ancient law of blood vengeance would demand Esau's execution as well. Her scheming had gained the blessing for Jacob, but it immediately brought fear, grief, and family separation.

Rebekah approached Isaac and complained that Esau's local Hittite wives were making her life miserable, asking what good her life would be if Jacob also married one of them. She used this real household grief as an excuse to send Jacob away safely without telling Isaac about Esau's murder plot. Her clever appeal convinced Isaac that Jacob needed to travel to her homeland to find a godly wife.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Modern scholars often regard this verse as the start of a different source story, in which Jacob leaves home simply to find a suitable wife rather than escaping Esau's anger.
